name: Controlling 2^1000 Parameters
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Number Too Big to Control
lesson.summary: A generic state of n qubits requires on the order of 2^n continuous numbers to fully describe, and skeptics point to this exponential blowup, exemplified by the roughly 2^1000 parameters needed for a modest 1000 qubit system, as evidence of an uncontrollable physical system, while defenders counter that no quantum computer is ever built by directly setting each of those numbers one at a time.
lesson.body:
Here is a piece of uncontroversial mathematics that both supporters and skeptics of quantum computing agree on. A system of n qubits lives in a Hilbert space of dimension 2^n, and a generic pure quantum state assigns a complex amplitude to each of the 2^n possible classical bit strings the qubits could represent. Fully writing down such a state takes on the order of 2^n complex numbers, roughly twice that many real numbers once split into real and imaginary parts, minus a couple for normalization and an unobservable global phase, negligible corrections at this scale. For n equal to 1000 qubits, a modest target next to the millions fault-tolerant algorithms are often estimated to need, that is roughly 2^1000 numbers, about 10 to the 301st power, dwarfing even the roughly 10 to the 80th power atoms estimated to exist in the observable universe.

This number is the vivid, quantitative core of the physics based skepticism the previous chapter introduced through Dyakonov's work. The argument runs: if specifying the state of a modest quantum computer takes more numbers than there are atoms in the universe, doesn't reliably preparing and maintaining that state require physically managing an equally vast collection of continuous degrees of freedom, all simultaneously, all correctly related, for the whole computation. Framed this way, the challenge sounds less like scaling up a digital chip, where each transistor is an independent addition, and more like holding a delicate, vast structure together without one piece drifting.

The standard reply is that this framing, while mathematically accurate about the size of the state description, conflates that description with what an experimenter has to do. A quantum computer is not built by dialing in 2^1000 separate numbers on some enormous panel. It is built from local gates acting on one or two qubits at a time, each specified by a handful of real parameters, such as a rotation angle, and a useful algorithm needs only a number of gates that grows polynomially, not exponentially, with qubit count. The exponentially large state is never written down, it emerges from a polynomial sized sequence of local instructions. Error correction reinforces the point: fault-tolerant protocols extract only limited classical syndromes, never a full readout of all 2^n amplitudes, avoiding an exponential problem to fix an exponential state.

Dyakonov style skeptics have a reasonable rejoinder, why this stays contested rather than settled. Granting that no one writes down or individually targets each amplitude, the physical system still has to behave, at every moment, as though all of them are simultaneously present, coherent, and correctly related, since that is what it means to be the state the algorithm needs. Small, uncontrolled interactions between supposedly independent qubits, crosstalk, stray couplings, correlated noise, could disturb this implicit structure in ways a polynomially sized gate description does not capture, echoing the correlated noise concern Kalai raises from a more mathematical angle.

This concept tests whether both sides can be held accurately at once. It is correct that a quantum algorithm's control instructions compress into polynomially many parameters, so the naive claim that you must control 2^1000 independent knobs overstates it. It is also an open question, unresolved at the relevant scale, whether real hardware can sustain the implicit coherence that description is meant to produce, once systems grow large enough for the correlated noise Kalai and Dyakonov each worry about to show up.
